Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit.

We represent: defendant insurer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that an insurer has no duty to defend where the complaint's allegations fall entirely within a policy exclusion.

Cite at least six decisions of the First Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
# ARGUMENT

## I. [INSURER] HAD NO DUTY TO DEFEND BECAUSE EVERY ALLEGATION IN THE UNDERLYING COMPLAINT FALLS WITHIN THE [__] EXCLUSION.

### A. The duty to defend is measured by comparing the complaint to the policy.

Under Massachusetts law, which governs here, whether an insurer must defend turns on the allegations of the underlying complaint and the language of the policy. *See Billings v. Commerce Ins. Co.*, 936 N.E.2d 408, 414 (Mass. 2010); *Boston Symphony Orchestra, Inc. v. Commercial Union Ins. Co.*, 545 N.E.2d 1156, 1158 (Mass. 1989). This Court applies that comparison directly. The question is whether the complaint's allegations are "reasonably susceptible" of an interpretation that states a claim covered by the policy. *Open Software Found., Inc. v. U.S. Fid. & Guar. Co.*, 307 F.3d 11, 14 (1st Cir. 2002); *Liberty Mut. Ins. Co. v. Metro. Life Ins. Co.*, 260 F.3d 54, 61 (1st Cir. 2001); *Merchants Ins. Co. of N.H. v. U.S. Fid. & Guar. Co.*, 143 F.3d 5, 8 (1st Cir. 1998). The insurer's obligation therefore does not depend on how the claimant labels its theories, or on what the insured says the facts may prove. It depends on the facts the complaint actually alleges.

### B. Where the alleged facts fall wholly within an exclusion, no duty to defend arises.

The reasonably-susceptible standard is generous to the insured, but it is not unlimited. It asks whether the complaint can fairly be read to state a covered claim. It does not ask whether a creative reader could imagine one. When the allegations, fairly read, describe only conduct or injury that the policy excludes, the complaint states no potentially covered claim and the duty to defend does not attach. *See Mount Vernon Fire Ins. Co. v. Visionaid, Inc.*, 477 F.3d 6, 9–10 (1st Cir. 2007) (comparing the complaint's factual allegations to the policy and the exclusions at issue); *Metro. Prop. & Cas. Ins. Co. v. Morrison*, 460 F.3d 52, 58–59 (1st Cir. 2006) (same); *Ferrara & DiMercurio, Inc. v. St. Paul Mercury Ins. Co.*, 240 F.3d 1, 5–6 (1st Cir. 2001) (same).

The insurer bears the burden of showing that an exclusion applies. *Billings*, 936 N.E.2d at 414. Exclusions are construed strictly against the insurer, but clear and unambiguous exclusions are enforced according to their plain terms. *Open Software*, 307 F.3d at 14–15; *Liberty Mut.*, 260 F.3d at 61–62. Courts do not rewrite unambiguous language to create coverage the parties did not bargain for.

### C. The Complaint alleges only conduct within the [__] Exclusion.

The [__] Exclusion removes from coverage [quote operative exclusion language]. [Insurer's] burden is met here because each count of the Complaint rests on the same excluded conduct. Count I alleges [__] (Compl. ¶¶ __). Count II alleges [__] (Compl. ¶¶ __). Count III alleges [__] (Compl. ¶¶ __). Each count, however styled, arises from the facts alleged in paragraphs [__], which describe [excluded conduct] and nothing else.

The Complaint does not allege any separate, independent fact that would support a covered claim. Where, as here, the legal theories differ but every one depends on the same excluded facts, changing the label does not take the claim outside the exclusion. *See Morrison*, 460 F.3d at 59; *Visionaid*, 477 F.3d at 10. Whether the exclusion applies depends on the origin and nature of the harm alleged, not on the cause of action pleaded.

### D. [Insured's] contrary arguments do not create a duty to defend.

[Insured] may argue that the Complaint could be amended, or that discovery might reveal facts outside the exclusion. But the duty to defend rests on the facts alleged, or on facts known to the insurer that bear on coverage. It does not rest on speculation about what a claimant might later plead. *See Merchants*, 143 F.3d at 8–9; *Liberty Mut.*, 260 F.3d at 61. The "reasonably susceptible" test requires a real possibility of coverage, not a theoretical one. [Insured] identifies no allegation, and none exists, that describes a claim outside the [__] Exclusion.

Nor does the rule that ambiguities are resolved against the insurer help [Insured]. That rule applies only where the policy is genuinely ambiguous. A policy is not ambiguous merely because the parties dispute its meaning. *Open Software*, 307 F.3d at 15. The exclusion here is clear, and it squarely covers the conduct alleged.

### E. Conclusion

Because the Complaint alleges only conduct that falls within the [__] Exclusion, [Insurer] owed no duty to defend. The district court's judgment should be [affirmed/reversed].
